results.translation: Shi Jue Ming (Stone Decision Bright) refers to the shell of the abalone (Haliotis diversicolor), classified under the category of shelled aquatic creatures [介部, Jiè Bù]. Li Shizhen describes it as salty in flavor and neutral in nature [鹹、平], and non-toxic. According to the Bencao Gangmu, it principally treats visual dimness and internal eye obstruction [青盲內障], clouding of the eyes by superficial visual obstructions [目翳], liver deficiency with hyperactive fire [肝虛火旺], redness and painful swelling of the eyes, and steaming bone fever with consumptive heat [骨蒸勞熱]. Li Shizhen emphasizes its primary virtue as the clearing of liver heat and the brightening of vision, making it a foundational remedy in classical ophthalmological treatment.

results.translation: Li Shizhen describes oyster shell (Mǔ Lì) as salty in flavor and slightly cold in nature, non-toxic, and belonging to the category of substances that calm the spirit and anchor yang. It is indicated for febrile disorders including cold-damage [shāng hán] with alternating chills and heat, malarial conditions, and pathological states of fright, rage, and emotional agitation. Li Shizhen further notes its capacity to soften hardness and disperse nodules [ruǎn jiān sàn jié], restrain yin and subdue ascending yang [liǎn yīn qián yáng], check spontaneous and night sweating, and astringe seminal emission; calcined and powdered, it may be applied topically to carbuncles and festering sores [yōng jū].

entities_mentioned.name: 牡蠣 (Mǔ Lì)
entities_mentioned.modern_identification: Ostrea gigas / Crassostrea gigas (Pacific oyster) or closely related Ostrea species; shell used medicinally
entities_mentioned.notes: The medicinal substance is the dried, often calcined shell, not the soft tissue. Multiple Ostrea and Crassostrea species were used interchangeably in classical Chinese materia medica. The shell is rich in calcium carbonate and is still used in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) today under the same name.

results.translation: Li Shizhen classifies the clam (蛤蜊, Gélí) as salty in flavor and cold in nature, with no toxicity. He states that it nourishes and moistens the five viscera [wǔ zàng], relieves excessive thirst [xiāo kě, analogous to wasting-thirst or diabetes-like conditions], stimulates appetite, and counteracts alcohol toxicity. The calcined shell [gélí ké huī] is additionally employed to clear heat, resolve and disperse phlegm nodules [huà tán sàn jié], soften hardness, and reduce swelling, making it applicable to abscesses, sores, and chronic accumulations of cold [lǎo pǐ].

entities_mentioned.notes: The whole animal is consumed medicinally or as food; the shell, once calcined, yields a calcium-rich ash (gélí fěn) used as a phlegm-transforming and softening agent. Taxonomically close to Cyclina sinensis, which shares overlapping traditional uses.

results.title_inferred: Tortoise Plastron (Gui Jia) — Nourishing Yin and Anchoring Yang
results.original_text: 龜甲 (Guī Jiǎ) — Testudo horsfieldi Gray. 龜甲味鹹、甘，平，無毒。主治漏下赤白，破癥瘕瘧疾，五痔陰蝕，濕痹四肢重弱，小兒囟不合。久服輕身不飢，益氣資智，亦使人能食。炙用。
results.translation: Tortoise plastron [龜甲, Guī Jiǎ], as described by Li Shizhen, is salty and sweet in flavor, neutral in nature [平], and non-toxic. It is indicated for abnormal uterine bleeding with red or white discharge, the breaking up of abdominal masses [癥瘕], malarial disorders, the five types of hemorrhoids, genital erosion, damp impediment [濕痹] with heaviness and weakness of the four limbs, and failure of the infant fontanelle to close. Li Shizhen further notes that prolonged use lightens the body, alleviates hunger, augments qi, sharpens the intellect, and improves appetite.

entities_mentioned.name: 龜甲 (Guī Jiǎ)
entities_mentioned.modern_identification: Plastrum Testudinis — plastron of Testudo horsfieldi Gray (Chinese tortoise); in modern TCM taxonomy more commonly sourced from Chinemys reevesii
entities_mentioned.notes: The plastron (ventral shell plate) is the medicinally active part. Li Shizhen classifies it under the Scales and Shells [介部] category. It remains a core yin-nourishing substance in Traditional Chinese Medicine and is included in the Chinese Pharmacopoeia.

entities_mentioned.modern_identification: Abdominal masses; possibly corresponding to uterine fibroids, ovarian cysts, or organomegaly

entities_mentioned.name: 濕痹 (Shī Bì)
entities_mentioned.modern_identification: Damp impediment; broadly correlates with rheumatic or arthritic conditions exacerbated by dampness

entities_mentioned.name: 囟不合 (Xìn Bù Hé)

entities_mentioned.notes: A pediatric condition in classical medicine linked to insufficiency of kidney essence [腎精], which Gui Jia was believed to supplement.

results.title_inferred: Chinese Softshell Turtle Carapace (Bie Jia)
results.original_text: 鱉甲 (Biē Jiǎ) — Trionyx sinensis. 鱉甲味鹹，性微寒，無毒。主心腹症瘕堅積，寒熱，去痞疾，息肉，陰蝕，痔核，惡肉。療溫瘧，血瘕，腰痛，小兒脅下堅。久服益氣。滋陰清熱，平肝熄風，軟堅散結。
results.translation: According to Li Shizhen, the carapace of the Chinese softshell turtle (鱉甲, Biē Jiǎ) is salty in flavor and slightly cold in nature, and is without toxicity [non-toxic]. It is indicated primarily for abdominal concretions [zhēng jiǎ, 症瘕], hardened accumulations, alternating chills and fever [deficiency-heat patterns], and is used to eliminate masses [pǐ jí, 痞疾], abnormal growths [息肉, polyps or fleshy excrescences], ulceration of the yin [genitourinary erosions], hemorrhoidal nodules, and malignant flesh [necrotic or pathological tissue]. Li Shizhen further notes its therapeutic value in warm-type malaria [wēn nüè, 溫瘧], blood accumulation [xuè jiǎ, 血瘕], lumbar pain, and hardness beneath the hypochondrium in children; prolonged use is said to augment qi, nourish yin, clear deficiency heat, calm the liver, extinguish wind [a classical Chinese medical concept denoting suppression of internal pathogenic wind], and soften hardness to disperse nodules [ruǎn jiān sàn jié, 軟堅散結].

entities_mentioned.name: 鱉甲 (Biē Jiǎ)
entities_mentioned.modern_identification: Trionyx sinensis — Chinese softshell turtle carapace (dried dorsal shell/plastron)
entities_mentioned.notes: Standard identification confirmed across traditional Chinese materia medica literature and modern pharmacopoeia (Chinese Pharmacopoeia 2020 includes Bie Jia). The carapace contains collagen, calcium carbonate, and amino acids. Modern research supports anti-tumor, immunomodulatory, and hepatoprotective activities consistent with classical indications.

entities_mentioned.modern_identification: Abdominal masses; possibly hepatosplenomegaly, tumors, or fibrotic accumulations
entities_mentioned.notes: A classical Chinese medical category broadly encompassing palpable abdominal concretions; not a single modern disease equivalent. Often associated with liver cirrhosis, splenomegaly, or gynecological masses in modern TCM clinical interpretation.

entities_mentioned.notes: A classical subcategory of malaria [nüè, 瘧] characterized by predominant heat over cold; Bie Jia is a key ingredient in classical anti-malarial formulas such as Bie Jia Jian Wan (鱉甲煎丸) described in the Jinkui Yaolue.

entities_mentioned.name: 軟堅散結 (Ruǎn Jiān Sàn Jié)
entities_mentioned.notes: A classical Chinese therapeutic action meaning 'to soften hardness and disperse nodules or masses.' Not a modern biomedical entity but a functional category; clinically applied to fibrotic, neoplastic, or lymphatic swellings.

results.preparation: The carapace is typically vinegar-calcined [醋炙, cù zhì] before use to enhance its ability to soften masses and improve absorption; raw carapace [生鱉甲, shēng biē jiǎ] is preferred for nourishing yin and clearing heat. Standard decoction dose in classical sources ranges from 9–30 g, broken into pieces and decocted prior to other herbs [先煎, xiān jiān]. May also be prepared as pills or powders. External application in powdered form is noted for hemorrhoidal and ulcerative conditions.

results.translation: Common carp (Lǐ Yú, Cyprinus carpio) is described by Li Shizhen as sweet in flavor [甘], neutral in nature [性平], and non-toxic [無毒]. It is indicated for counterflow cough and uprising qi [咳逆上氣], jaundice [黃疸], and the relief of thirst. When consumed fresh or raw, it is said to address water swelling [水腫] and fullness of the legs [腳滿], and to descend qi [下氣]; when cooked, it treats water-qi floating edema [水氣浮腫] and promotes urination [利小便]. Li Shizhen further notes its use in calming fetal restlessness [胎動] in pregnant women, stabilizing the fetus [安胎], underscoring carp's longstanding role in obstetric dietary medicine within the classical tradition.

results.original_text: 鰻鱺 (Mán lí) — 本草綱目, 李時珍, 1596年。鰻鱺，補虛羸，殺諸蟲，治骨蒸勞瘵。其肉甘平，無毒。
results.translation: The eel (鰻鱺, Mán lí; Clarias batrachus or commonly Anguilla species) is described by Li Shizhen as having a sweet [甘] and balanced [平] flavor and nature, and is considered non-toxic. Li Shizhen records that it supplements [補] vacuity and emaciation [虛羸], kills various parasites [殺諸蟲], and is indicated for bone-steaming taxation illness [骨蒸勞瘵], a classical Chinese medical designation closely associated with what would today be recognized as pulmonary tuberculosis or consumptive wasting conditions. The eel is thus classified among nourishing animal-based medicinals employed to restore constitutional deficiency and address chronic debilitating disease.

The silkworm chrysalis (cán yǒng) is considered sweet and warm, tonifying the middle burner [補中益氣], alleviating thirst, and aiding digestion, while the broader category of silkworm preparations is noted by Li Shizhen for its ability to stop convulsions [止痙] and resolve phlegm [化痰].
